title: Short-term vs. long-term memory
notes: A model remembers nothing between calls; your code decides what it sees each time.
Short-term memory is this conversation's messages; long-term memory is what you save and load later, like preferences and past orders.
Store the least data that does the job: never payment details, and no personal data you don't need.

slides.title: Short-term vs. long-term memory
slides.sub: What Scout remembers, what it forgets, and what it should never keep
sentences: Welcome to Module 4: memory, planning and reasoning.
In this lesson you will see why a model forgets everything between calls, and the two kinds of memory that fix it.
You will also learn what Scout should never remember, which matters just as much.

slides.title: Every call starts from zero

messages.label: Ravi
messages.text: Hi, my order is ORB-10533. Has the sleeping bag shipped?

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: Thanks, Ravi. Let me check order ORB-10533 for you.

messages.label: Next call
messages.text: Sent this time: only Ravi's new question. The earlier messages were left out.

messages.label: Ravi
messages.text: And the foam mat, is that in the same parcel?

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: Happy to help! Could you give me your order number?

aside.label: Stateless
aside.text: The API keeps nothing between calls. Memory lives in your code, not in the model.

sentences: Let's start with the most surprising fact about language models.
Ravi gives Scout his order number, and Scout uses it in its reply.
On the next call, imagine your code sends only Ravi's new question, and leaves the earlier messages out.
Scout asks for the order number, as if it had never seen it.
That's because the model keeps nothing between calls. Each call starts from a blank page.
Whatever the model needs to know, your code has to send it, every single time.

slides.title: So what is agent memory?
slides.definition: Information your code keeps and sends back to the model, so it can use what it learned earlier.

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: A busy doctor's notes. She can't recall every patient, so she reads the notes on her desk before each visit.

sentences: So when people say an agent has memory, what do they mean?
Memory is information that your code keeps, outside the model.
Before each call, your code sends the useful parts back to the model.
It comes in two kinds: short-term memory for this conversation, and long-term memory that lasts across conversations.
Think of a busy doctor. She can't recall every patient, so she reads the notes on her desk before each visit.

slides.title: Two kinds of memory

left.label: Short-term memory
points: Example: what Ravi said two turns ago

right.label: Long-term memory
points: Saved in a file or database
Loaded when the customer comes back
Example: Ana prefers green; her past orders

sentences: Here are the two kinds side by side.
Short-term memory is the conversation itself: the list of messages you send with every call.
It's what lets Scout know what Ravi said two turns ago.
When the chat ends, it's gone, and that is usually fine.
Long-term memory is what you choose to save in a file or a database, and load next time.
Think of a customer's preferences, like Ana always choosing green, or the list of her past orders.
It survives between conversations, so Scout can greet a returning customer with context.

slides.title: How memory reaches the model

note.text: The model only knows what is inside this one request.

sentences: Let's follow one turn and see where memory fits.
A customer sends a message.
Your code loads long-term memory, such as her profile and her past orders.
It builds the request: the system prompt, that memory, and the short-term messages so far.
The model reads everything in the request and writes a reply.
Then your code saves the new turn, and any fact worth keeping.
Remember, the model only ever knows what is inside this one request.

slides.title: What should Scout keep?

note.text: Keep only what helps the next answer. Every stored detail is something to protect.

sentences: Not everything a customer says is worth remembering.
The order number in this chat? Yes. It lives in the messages, and Scout needs it until the chat ends.
A preferred colour or size? Worth saving to her profile, if it makes the next visit easier.
Past orders already live in Orbit's order system, so Scout loads them from there instead of keeping its own copy.
Card numbers, passwords and security codes? Never store them, anywhere. Mask them before anything is saved.
And don't collect personal details just in case. If Scout doesn't need it, don't keep it.
Every detail you store is something you must protect, and something that could leak.

slides.title: Three memory mistakes
sentences: Builders tend to make one of three memory mistakes.
The first is remembering nothing: the code forgets to send the history.
The customer has to repeat herself, and that is exactly how trust is lost.
The second is remembering everything: the whole history, on every call, forever.
That gets slow and expensive, and the next lesson shows you how to fix it.
The third is trusting stale facts, like an address saved last year.
For anything that can change, look it up fresh from the source, or confirm it with the customer.

slides.title: What to take away

points.text: A model keeps nothing between calls. Your code is the memory.
Short-term memory is the conversation, sent again with every call.
Long-term memory is saved and loaded: preferences, past orders.
Never store payment details, or personal data you don't need.

sentences: Let's recap.
A model keeps nothing between calls, so memory always lives in your code.
Short-term memory is the conversation, sent again with every call.
Long-term memory is what you save and load later, like preferences and past orders.
And the safest data is data you never stored: no payment details, and nothing you don't need.
Next, you will see what short-term memory costs as a conversation grows.

midQuiz.q: Scout's second API call sends only the customer's new question. What does the model know about the first call?
options: Everything, because it remembers the session
Nothing; it only sees what this call sends
Only the last reply it wrote
midQuiz.explain: The API keeps nothing between calls. If earlier messages matter, your code has to send them again.
midQuiz.hint: Where does memory live: inside the model, or in your code?

midQuiz.q: Ana has chosen green gear on her last three orders. Where should that preference live?
options: In short-term memory, the messages of this chat
In long-term memory, saved and loaded on her next visit
Nowhere; the model will notice it by itself
midQuiz.explain: This chat will end, but the preference is still useful next month. That is what long-term memory is for.
midQuiz.hint: Will this conversation still exist the next time Ana writes in?

endQuiz.q: A customer pastes his card number into the chat. What should Scout's memory do with it?
options: Save it so he doesn't need to type it again
Mask it before anything is saved, and never store it
Keep it in long-term memory, which only Scout can read
endQuiz.explain: Scout never needs a card number, so storing it adds risk and no value. Mask it before anything is saved or logged.
endQuiz.hint: Which of Scout's jobs actually needs a card number?

endQuiz.q: Which of these should Scout load from Orbit's order system rather than keep its own copy of?
options: The order number given two messages ago
endQuiz.explain: Past orders already have an official home, and their status changes. Load them when needed instead of keeping a copy that goes stale.
endQuiz.hint: Which of these already lives somewhere official, and keeps changing?
